items.summary: Abstract Compact models of memristors are essential for simulating large-scale neuromorphic systems, yet they often do not include description of complex dynamics like volatile relaxation and synaptic plasticity. We introduce a modular, computationally efficient memristor model that bridges this gap by integrating principles from physics and computational neuroscience. items.title: Neural Representation of Hedonic Valence During Narrative Listening
items.summary: Abstract Hedonic valence, the intrinsic pleasantness or unpleasantness of an experience, is fundamental to human psychological functioning. Yet, how valence is represented in the brain remains an open question. Functional MRI studies have demonstrated that the brain encodes both positive and negative valence, but this evidence largely stems from experiments using simplified, controlled stimuli, such as images, sounds, or words. items.title: Understanding stress from a cultural perspective: the role of self-construal
items.summary: Stress is an adaptive psychophysiological process that plays an important role in human survival and adjustment. Increasing evidence suggests that stress responses are shaped not only by environmental demands but also by cultural and self-related psychological processes. items.title: Neuroscience, Neurocentrism, Neuromania, and Neurophobia: When New Knowledge Challenges Established Ways of Knowing
items.summary: Advances in neuroscience have transformed our understanding of the brain and human behavior, while also generating new ethical, philosophical, and social debates. This commentary explores neurocentrism, neuromania, neurophobia, and neurocriticism as contrasting perspectives on the growing influence of neuroscientific knowledge. A balanced and interdisciplinary approach is essential to avoid both reductionist interpretations and unjustified skepticism, while preserving the complexity of the human mind and promoting critical, evidence-based scientific communication.

items.title: Behavioral techniques for controlling visual stimuli to modulate visual processing in the brain and their implementation in augmented reality technology
items.summary: This study reviews the behavioral techniques that control visual stimuli to systematically modulate visual processing in an observer’s brain. These techniques are indirect but more affordable than more-direct techniques for stimulating the brain. The limitations of these techniques and the calibrations necessary for them are also discussed. Some of the behavioral techniques can be also used in field studies by making use of Augmented Reality (AR) technology and a head-mounted display (HMD).
